Who posts a quote and why a venue would pay for one is the mechanism in how it works today.
A prediction market contract pays one of two amounts when it resolves, so size still open
at the end jumps to a full payout or to zero. That settlement exposure is a different control problem
from quoting a stock or a future you can roll. The number on the screen is a probability,
and the quote is what turns an incoming order into an update of that probability. A paper on archive,
optimal market making and prediction markets, models that price as a conditional probability generated
by transforming a latent belief that defuses over time. The market maker picks a bid and an ask
to maximize expected wealth at the end. Marked to market inventory risk while the market is open,
and settlement risk on contracts left open at resolution, sit in the same problem.
The authors derive the Hamilton-Jakoby-Bellman equation and characterize a unique optimal bid and a
unique optimal ask. Shifting the equation into latent belief space and using a fixed point argument,
they prove a classical solution exists and is unique, and they verify that the quoting rule from it
is optimal. Their comparison has no dollar figures in the abstract. A myopic quota maximizes
only the instantaneous expected mark-to-market profit. The edge on the next trade marked
at the new probability. The optimal rule also has to care how inventory behaves if the
latent belief keeps moving and how that inventory pays if the event resolves either way.
Inventory shifts the quote because a maker already longed the yes side is less willing
to buy more of it and more willing to sell it.
Market beliefs shift the quote because the latent probability is the thing being marked.
Time to resolution shifts the quote because settlement risk dominates when the binary
payoff is close, and mark to market risk has longer to compound when resolution is far.
Risk aversion changes how hard those penalties bite, so a more risk averse maker posts
a wider quote or a sharper inventory skew for the same book.
Against that myopic benchmark, the paper finds the optimal strategy substantially improves
downside protection while preserving most expected profit.

asks how much liquidity the mechanism itself supplies.
